diagnostic_evidence.quote: demonstrating the accuracy and efficiency of these methods, based entirely on the classical separation of variables technique

This efficiency arises from decomposing the original problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved independently using separation of variables, significantly reducing the computational cost, especially for high-dimensional systems.
Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) against RK45 method with tolerance $10^{-16}$

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and conclusion advertise efficiency: the splitting method is claimed to be 'more computationally efficient' than RK45 and to 'significantly reduc[e] the computational cost'. The paper contains no runtime measurements, operation counts, or per-step cost comparisons of any kind; every quantitative comparison with RK45 is an RMSE (accuracy) value with RK45 used merely as a reference solution. The only complexity evidence in the paper (Table tabNterms) shows the number of exponential evaluations per step growing as high as 8193, and that cost is never compared to the cost of an RK45 step. The efficiency guarantee is therefore unsupported by anything in the source.

failure_location.quote: the splitting method is not only competitive in accuracy but also more computationally efficient.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Delete or qualify the efficiency claims so that only accuracy/RMSE conclusions are drawn (or supply actual timing/cost comparisons); no formal result needs modification.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised practical advantage over Runge-Kutta (abstract and Section sec:conclusions) is unsubstantiated; all theorems and all RMSE accuracy results are unaffected.
issues.title: Abstract and conclusion claim computational efficiency over RK45 without any cost evidence
issues.why_classification: No evidence in the source can support the efficiency guarantee, so the least repair withdraws an advertised comparative claim; this is a limited weakening that leaves every theorem and all accuracy numerics intact, i.e., more than a local fix but with a recognizably comparable paper surviving.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: See \cite{JD3}.
and most importantly for our purposes the work of Franziska K\"uhnemund \cite{JD3} in which she extends the result to the bi-continuous case.

issues.failure_explanation: The introduction lists, as the paper's second main advance, the extension of Chernoff's product formula to bi-continuous semigroups, pointing to Theorem CPFBi. But Theorem CPFBi is stated for an arbitrary bi-admissible Banach space and its entire proof is the citation 'See [JD3]', and the body text itself credits Kühnemund [JD3] with extending Chernoff's result to the bi-continuous case. What the paper actually adds is the application of that quoted theorem to Koopman semigroups on C_b(Ω) (Eq. (Arun)) and the pointwise-convergence corollary (Proposition Frank); no separate proof of 'well-posedness and contraction of the splitting operators' is given. The advance as stated is materially misleading about what the paper establishes.

failure_location.quote: \textit{Bi-continuous Chernoff extension}. We extend Chernoff's product formula to bicontinuous semigroups on bounded continuous functions arising from nonlinear flows, proving well-posedness and contraction of the splitting operators (Theorem \ref{CPFBi}).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reword the advance to attribute the bi-continuous Chernoff extension to Kühnemund [JD3] and claim only the application to C_b(Ω) Koopman semigroups (Eq. (Arun), Proposition Frank) as the paper's contribution.
issues.overall_effect: One of the four advertised main advances is a cited result of [JD3]; the mathematical content used downstream remains valid, but the novelty claim must shrink to the specialization to nonlinear-flow Koopman semigroups on C_b(Ω).
issues.title: Kühnemund's bi-continuous Chernoff product formula advertised as the paper's own extension
issues.why_classification: A short, local rewording of attribution preserves every theorem and guarantee; the quoted theorem remains available by citation and no mathematical content is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: has 7 terms and is of order 4, where $a= 0.324396 + 0.134586 i$.

issues.failure_explanation: For the symmetric triple composition in (HO53) to raise the order from 2k to 2k+2, the leading error term forces 2a_k^{2k+1}+(1-2a_k)^{2k+1}=0, whose relevant roots are a_k=1/(2+2^{1/(2k+1)}e^{±iπ/(2k+1)}). The displayed closed form instead solves (1-a_k)^{2k+1}=-2a_k^{2k+1}; for k=1 it evaluates to approximately 0.4237+0.2836i, which neither equals the paper's own printed decimal a=0.324396+0.134586i (a correct root: 2a^3+(1-2a)^3≈0) nor annihilates the degree-(2k+1) error term. With the formula as printed, W_{[1]} is only of order 2 (in general 2k), contradicting the stated order 2k+2; the analogy to [JD6] Theorem 2.3 supports the claim only for the corrected coefficient.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the formula by a_k = e^{π i/(2k+1)}/(2e^{π i/(2k+1)}+2^{1/(2k+1)}) = 1/(2+2^{1/(2k+1)}e^{-π i/(2k+1)}), i.e., insert the missing factor 2 in the denominator; this is forced by the order condition and matches the paper's own decimals.
issues.overall_effect: The general formula defining the W_{[k]} coefficients is false; the printed decimal constants for k=1,2,3 (the only cases in scope and the ones used downstream) are correct, so instantiated schemes survive, but any reader instantiating the closed form obtains a method of order 2k instead of 2k+2.
issues.title: Closed-form coefficient a_k for the W-family violates the order condition
issues.why_classification: The correction is a single forced local edit pinned down by the order condition and by the paper's own correct decimals; every substantive claim (orders, term counts, algorithms) is preserved and no new argument is needed.

issues.failure_explanation: Expanding the defining recursion W_{[k]}(t)=W_{[k-1]}(a_kt)W_{[k-1]}((1-2a_k)t)W_{[k-1]}(a_kt) with W_{[0]}=e^{t/2 K_2}e^{tK_1}e^{t/2 K_2} shows the printed expansions are wrong: (i) in W_{[1]} the fifth factor must be e^{(1-a)t/2 K_2} (the junction of e^{(1-2a)t/2 K_2} and e^{at/2 K_2}), not e^{(1-a)t K_2}; as printed the K_2-coefficients sum to (3-a)/2 ≠ 1, so the displayed W_{[1]} is not even a consistent (order-1) splitting. (ii) In W_{[2]} both factors e^{(a+b)t K_2} must be e^{(a+b)t/2 K_2}, and the middle K_1-coefficient must be d=(1-2a_1)(1-2a_2)≈0.1637-0.0422i, not the printed d=1-2a≈0.8098-0.1357i (the adjacent factors e^{(c+d)t/2 K_2} are correct only with the right d). (iii) In W_{[3]} the printed constants d=0.034783-0.043571i and h=0.0137277-0.060005i do not equal the required products (1-2a_1)(1-2a_2)a_3≈0.0555-0.0052i and (1-2a_1)(1-2a_2)(1-2a_3)≈0.0527-0.0318i, and the same missing factor 1/2 recurs in the K_2-junctions. The recursion (HO53) and the first-level constants (a≈0.324396+0.134586i, etc.) are correct, so the stated orders (2k+2) and term counts (2·3^k+1) hold for the recursively defined schemes; only the explicit displays are false.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Re-expand the displays mechanically from (HO53): halve the doubled junction coefficients and replace d and h by the correct products (1-2a_1)(1-2a_2)[a_3] and (1-2a_1)(1-2a_2)(1-2a_3).
issues.overall_effect: The explicit formulas for the 4th-, 6th-, and 8th-order W-schemes are unreliable as printed; a reader implementing them obtains methods that are inconsistent or of reduced order. The existence, order, and term-count claims of Theorem thm:added-1 survive via the recursion; nothing downstream uses these displays.
issues.title: Explicit W_{[1]}, W_{[2]}, W_{[3]} expansions contain coefficients inconsistent with their defining recursion
issues.why_classification: The repair is routine substitution into an already-correct recursive definition; no new lemma or construction is needed and every substantive claim (orders, term counts, downstream algorithms) is preserved.

issues.failure_explanation: Expanding Z_{[2]}(t)=Z_{[1]}(a_2t)Z_{[1]}(\bar a_2t)Z_{[1]}(\bar a_2t)Z_{[1]}(a_2t) with the (correct) printed Z_{[1]} shows: with a=a_1a_2 and b=\bar a_1a_2 one has (\bar a+\bar b)/2=\bar a_2/4 and (a+\bar b)/2=a_1/4, so each middle factor of the two \bar a_2-blocks is a single e^{(\bar a+\bar b)t/2 K_2}, and the final junction is e^{(a+\bar b)t/2 K_2}. The display instead prints e^{(\bar a+\bar b)t K_2} four times and e^{(a+\bar b)t K_2} once (the first junction e^{(a+\bar b)t/2 K_2} is printed correctly, confirming the intended pattern). As printed, the K_2-exponents sum to 1+2 Re(\bar a+\bar b)+Re(a+\bar b)/2 = 1.3125 ≠ 1, so the displayed 33-term composition is not even a consistent (order-1) splitting, let alone of order 6; the order-6 claim holds only for the scheme defined by the recursion (HO533).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Halve the five offending exponents (the four (\bar a+\bar b)t factors and the one (a+\bar b)t factor), as dictated by expanding (HO533).
issues.overall_effect: The explicit Z_{[2]} formula (order 6, 33 terms) is false as printed and, if implemented, yields a non-convergent 'splitting'; the recursion (HO533), the printed constants a,b, and the order/term-count claims are unaffected.
issues.title: Displayed 33-term Z_{[2]} expansion has five doubled K_2 exponents and is not a consistent splitting
issues.why_classification: A forced local correction of five exponents against the paper's own correct recursion restores the claim; no new argument and no loss of content.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \STATE \textbf{Input:} Let \( x \) be the number of exponential terms for \( N = 2 \)

issues.failure_explanation: Starting from the N=2 count x, each substitution iteration raises the dimension by one: with x=5, iteration 1 prints 13 (the N=3 value) and iteration 2 prints 25 (N=4), exactly matching the paper's own Table tabNterms. Hence the count for dimension N is obtained after N-2 iterations, but the loop runs i=1..N-1, so the final printed total for input N is the count for dimension N+1 (e.g., for N=3 the last printed Sum is 25 instead of the correct 13). The algorithm's input-output contract 'total number of terms for dimension N' fails by one dimension.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the loop bound to i=1..N-2 (or relabel the printed iteration-to-dimension mapping).
issues.overall_effect: As written, the algorithm's final output for dimension N is the (N+1)-dimensional term count; the published table values correspond to the corrected reading (iteration i ↔ dimension i+2), so the table itself is unaffected.
issues.title: Exponential-term counting algorithm iterates one step too many
issues.why_classification: A one-token loop-bound correction restores the stated contract; the computed values and the table derived from them are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: has 17 terms, and is of order 5, where
has 19 terms, and is of order 6, where
has 33 terms, and is of order 6, where

issues.failure_explanation: The row labeled p=6 uses a two-dimensional count of 17 exponential terms, but the paper contains no 17-term order-6 scheme: its only 17-term scheme, U_{[3]}, is stated in Theorem splitU to be of order 5, while the paper's order-6 schemes have 19 (W_{[2]}) or 33 (U_{[4]}, Z_{[2]}) terms. The remaining entries (145, 289, 1313, 2465, 3617, 4913) are exactly what the algorithm of alg:added-1 generates from input x=17, so the entire row counts the N-dimensional extensions of an order-5 scheme (or of an unspecified scheme) while being labeled 6th order. Since none of the experiments identify which scheme their '6th' columns used, it is also undetermined from the source whether the reported '6th'-order RMSE values (three tables) were produced by an order-6 method at all.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either relabel the row as the order-5 family, or recompute it from a genuine order-6 scheme (e.g., x=19 for W_{[2]}, giving 19, 181, 361, ...), and identify or relabel the scheme behind the '6th' columns of the experiments accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The order-6 row of Table tabNterms and all counts derived from it are mislabeled or unsupported; the '6th' columns of the three RMSE tables and the conclusion's statements about 6th-order performance rest on an unidentified scheme whose order cannot be confirmed from the source.
issues.title: Order-6 row of the term-count table counts a 17-term scheme that the paper itself classifies as order 5
issues.why_classification: The fix is contained (recompute or relabel one row) but is not a typo: the counts must be regenerated from a chosen order-6 scheme, and the ambiguity extends to the order labels of the experimental results and the conclusion's 6th-order performance claims, a limited weakening with no theorem lost.

issues.failure_explanation: The iteration in Remark remApp (c) is meant to apply the five factors of V_3(t/n) in succession, so the second x-update (the factor e^{a t K_1}) must start from x_{k+\bar a} produced in step (2) (the factor e^{\bar a t K_1}). Step (4) instead starts from the stale x_k, discarding step (2)'s update entirely; the map (x_k,y_k)↦(x_{k+1},y_{k+1}) as written is therefore not the composition V_3(t/n), and the claimed accuracy C t^4/n^3 does not hold for the written iteration.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace x_k by x_{k+\bar a} in step (4): x_{k+1}=σ_{y_{k+1/2}}(ta/n, x_{k+\bar a}).
issues.overall_effect: The explicit third-order algorithm of Remark remApp (c) does not implement Proposition prop333's V_3 as written; its stated t^4/n^3 order guarantee is unsupported for the displayed iteration (the corrected iteration restores it).
issues.title: Third-order 2D algorithm starts the second x-update from the stale value x_k
issues.why_classification: A single forced argument correction, dictated by the composition structure and the surrounding steps (step (2) is dead code otherwise), restores the stated guarantee with no other change.
